title: Parenthood and the Gender Earnings Gap
text:
The gender earnings gap is a persistent feature of the U.S. labor market, but the size of the gap may differ across workers with different family circumstances. In this post, I use data from the 2025 Annual Social and Economic Supplement (ASEC) of the Current Population Survey to examine whether the gender earnings gap differs between workers with and without children in the household.
Rather than estimating the causal effect of parenthood, this analysis provides a descriptive comparison of earnings and work patterns across men and women with and without children in the household.

title: Parenthood and the Gender Earnings Gap
text:
The gender earnings gap is a persistent feature of the U.S. labor market, but the size of the gap may differ across workers with different family circumstances. In this post, I use data from the 2025 Annual Social and Economic Supplement (ASEC) of the Current Population Survey to examine whether the gender earnings gap differs between workers with and without children in the household.
Rather than estimating the causal effect of parenthood, this analysis provides a descriptive comparison of earnings and work patterns across men and women with and without children in the household.

title: Parenthood and the Gender Earnings Gap
text:
Data and Methods
The data come from the 2025 CPS ASEC, accessed through IPUMS CPS. I restrict the sample to adults ages 25 to 54 with positive wage and salary income who usually worked at least 35 hours per week and worked at least 50 weeks during the previous year. After these restrictions, the analysis sample contains 34,996 individuals.
Parenthood is defined using the number of one’s own children living in the household (NCHILD). Individuals with at least one own child in the household are classified as parents, while those with no own children in the household are classified as having no children.
I use the CPS ASEC person weight (ASECWT) to calculate weighted mean wage and salary income. I also compare usual weekly hours and weeks worked across the four groups to examine whether differences in work time accompany the observed earnings differences.

title: Parenthood and the Gender Earnings Gap
text:
Results
The earnings comparison shows a clear difference by parenthood status. Among workers without children in the household, weighted mean annual wage and salary income is $85,376 for men and $76,826 for women, corresponding to a gender earnings gap of about 10%. Among parents, mean income is $112,339 for men and $79,745 for women, producing a much larger gap of about 29%.
The difference is driven primarily by the substantially higher average earnings of fathers. Compared with men without children, fathers earn about $27,000 more on average, while the difference between mothers and women without children is much smaller, at about $3,000.









Weekly work hours differ only modestly across the four groups. Men without children work an average of 42.8 hours per week, compared with 41.8 hours for women without children. Among parents, men work about 43.8 hours per week, while women work about 41.8 hours. All four groups worked approximately 52 weeks during the previous year. These patterns suggest that differences in weeks worked are unlikely to explain the substantially larger earnings gap among parents, although differences in weekly hours may contribute somewhat.









Expressed directly as a percentage gap, the contrast is substantial: women without children earn about 10% less than men without children on average, while women who are parents earn about 29% less than men who are parents. The much larger gap among parents is therefore driven mainly by the sharp increase in men’s average earnings associated with parenthood in this descriptive comparison.

title: Parenthood and the Gender Earnings Gap
text:
Conclusion
Using the 2025 CPS ASEC, this analysis finds that the gender earnings gap among full-year workers differs substantially by parenthood status. The gap is about 10% among workers without children in the household, compared with about 29% among parents. This larger gap mainly reflects substantially higher average earnings among fathers, while mothers’ average earnings are only modestly higher than those of women without children.
These results are descriptive rather than causal. Parenthood may be associated with other differences in occupation, industry, education, work experience, or other characteristics that are not accounted for here. Nevertheless, the comparison illustrates how the gender earnings gap can vary considerably across workers with different family circumstances.

title: One Economy, Three Measures: Why Can GDP Be Measured Three Ways?
text:
Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is one of the most familiar measures in economics. But there is something about GDP accounting that initially seems strange: economists can calculate GDP in three different ways—the production approach, the expenditure approach, and the income approach—and, in principle, obtain exactly the same answer.
At first, these approaches seem to measure completely different things. The production approach asks how much value an economy produces. The expenditure approach asks how much is spent on final goods and services. The income approach asks how much income is generated in the production process. Why should these three numbers be equal?

title: One Economy, Three Measures: Why Can GDP Be Measured Three Ways?
text:
Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is one of the most familiar measures in economics. But there is something about GDP accounting that initially seems strange: economists can calculate GDP in three different ways—the production approach, the expenditure approach, and the income approach—and, in principle, obtain exactly the same answer.
At first, these approaches seem to measure completely different things. The production approach asks how much value an economy produces. The expenditure approach asks how much is spent on final goods and services. The income approach asks how much income is generated in the production process. Why should these three numbers be equal?

title: One Economy, Three Measures: Why Can GDP Be Measured Three Ways?
text:
Following One Transaction
Consider a simple example. Suppose I buy a loaf of bread from a bakery for $5. From the expenditure side, this is straightforward: I have spent $5 on a final consumption good, so it contributes $5 to consumption.
From the production side, we measure the value added in producing the bread. If the bakery uses $2 of flour produced by another firm and sells the bread for $5, the bakery adds $3 of value. The flour producer contributes the other $2. Across the whole production chain, total value added is therefore still $5. This is why GDP counts value added rather than simply adding up every transaction: otherwise intermediate goods such as flour would be counted twice.
Finally, the value created through production generates income. Across the entire production chain, the $5 of value added ultimately appears as income, such as wages and profits. Thus, the same economic activity appears as $5 of production, $5 of expenditure, and $5 of income.
\[
\text{Production} = \text{Expenditure} = \text{Income}
\]

title: One Economy, Three Measures: Why Can GDP Be Measured Three Ways?
section: What If Nobody Buys the Bread?
text:
What If Nobody Buys the Bread?
Now consider a less intuitive case. Suppose the $5 loaf is produced, but nobody buys it before the end of the accounting period. Has GDP fallen by $5?
No. The production approach has not changed: the bread was still produced during the period. What changes is its classification under the expenditure approach. Instead of appearing as $5 of consumption, the unsold bread is recorded as $5 of inventory investment. Therefore, total GDP is unchanged.
\[
C \downarrow \$5,\qquad I_{\text{inventory}} \uparrow \$5
\]
The income approach also remains consistent. Income generated by production does not require the final product to have already been sold for cash. The unsold bread becomes an inventory asset of the firm. In national accounting, what matters is that production occurred during the period.
This reveals an important distinction: GDP measures current production, not simply current sales or cash receipts.

title: One Economy, Three Measures: Why Can GDP Be Measured Three Ways?
text:
The Takeaway
The three approaches to GDP are not three unrelated ways of estimating the economy. They are three perspectives on the same economic activity. Production creates value, expenditure purchases final output, and the production process generates income.
Once we follow a transaction through the economy, the identity becomes much less mysterious:
\[
\boxed{\text{Production} = \text{Expenditure} = \text{Income}}
\]
The equality is not a coincidence. It is built into the way economic transactions connect buyers, producers, and income earners.

title: Growth, Job Openings, and Entry Barriers: Exploring Bright Outlook Careers
text: Choosing a career involves more than simply looking for occupations with high projected growth. A rapidly growing occupation may still offer relatively few openings, while an occupation with many openings may require very different levels of education, experience, and training. In this post, I use data from O*NET OnLine to explore how promising career opportunities are distributed across different levels of job preparation. Specifically, I ask: **How do rapid-growth and high-opening occupations differ across O*NET Job Zones, and what does this suggest about the relationship between career opportunities and entry barriers?**

title: Growth, Job Openings, and Entry Barriers: Exploring Bright Outlook Careers
Growth, Job Openings, and Entry Barriers: Exploring Bright Outlook Careers
text:
Results
The distribution of Bright Outlook occupations differs noticeably across Job Zones. Rapid-growth occupations appear in every preparation level, but they are especially common in Job Zones 3 and 4. Job Zone 4 contains the largest number of rapid-growth occupations, suggesting that many expanding careers require considerable preparation rather than either minimal preparation or the highest level of specialization.
A more informative pattern emerges when I focus on occupations that satisfy both Bright Outlook criteria: rapid growth and numerous job openings. Among these 32 occupations, 46.9% are in Job Zone 4, the largest share, while 34.4% are in Job Zones 1–2. Job Zone 3 accounts for 12.5%, and only 6.2% are in Job Zone 5. This suggests that strong employment opportunities are not concentrated at a single level of preparation.

title: Growth, Job Openings, and Entry Barriers: Exploring Bright Outlook Careers
text:
Conclusion
This analysis shows that strong career outlooks exist across a wide range of preparation levels. Although Job Zone 4 contains the largest share of occupations combining rapid growth with numerous openings, more than one-third of these occupations are in Job Zones 1–2. This suggests that workers do not necessarily need the highest level of education, experience, and training to enter occupations with favorable employment prospects.
For job seekers, the practical takeaway is to consider both expected growth and the number of openings rather than focusing on either measure alone. Job Zone can then be used as an additional filter for the amount of preparation required. This provides a simple way to identify career opportunities that better match an individual’s current qualifications and willingness to invest in additional training.
